And you will meet an even bigger version of the same idea, from a different author.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, who made this claim, and when.
In nineteen ninety one, German editor Heribert Illig first proposed that centuries were missing from our calendar.
He popularized it further in nineteen ninety six, with a book published through his own small press.
He kept writing about it for years, through his own magazine. Documented.
Here is the actual claim.
Illig said two hundred ninety seven years, from the year six fourteen to nine eleven, were invented and inserted into our calendar.
Subtract that number from today, and by his logic we would be living closer to the year seventeen twenty nine.
That stretch covers the entire Carolingian period, including Charlemagne's famous coronation, in the year eight hundred.
This is what the theory claims, not what happened.
And here is who Illig blamed for it.
He accused two real historical figures, an emperor and a pope, of faking the calendar to place themselves symbolically at the year one thousand.
That is the accusation of the theory. It is not a historical fact about either man.
Illig built his case on a specific piece of math.
In fifteen eighty two, the Gregorian calendar reform corrected a drift of ten days.
By Illig's own count, starting from the year one, almost thirteen days should have piled up by then.
He read that three day gap as proof that nearly three hundred years never existed.
Here is where the whole theory breaks.
The Gregorian reform was never meant to fix the calendar back to the year one.
It was meant to return the calendar to where it stood at the Council of Nicaea, in the year three twenty five.
Count the drift from three twenty five instead, and the ten days correct themselves exactly. The theory's starting point was simply wrong.
And the math problem is not the only issue.
European writers before the year six hundred described solar eclipses, including one noted by the Roman author Pliny the Elder, in the year fifty nine.
Modern astronomical calculations place those eclipses on the exact same dates the old writers recorded.
Tree ring records from that period are also continuous, with no three hundred year gap anywhere.
Independent clocks in the sky and in the forest both agree: the centuries were never missing.
So how did historians respond?
The theory was rejected, essentially across the board, starting with a formal academic debate in nineteen ninety seven.
Even a researcher who once supported a related version of the idea walked away from it himself, in twenty eleven.
The rejection has held for nearly thirty years. Documented.
And if three hundred missing years sounds bold, it is not even the most extreme version.
A separate author, a Russian mathematician, claimed closer to one thousand years of history across multiple civilizations were fabricated.
Different author, different number, same rejected structure. The two theories should never be treated as one.
Let's count what we actually know.
Who proposed it, and when: documented.
The reference point that breaks the whole argument: documented.
The claim that any years actually went missing: a myth, not an open mystery.
So did we really lose two hundred ninety seven years?
No. We lost a correct reference point, in someone's math, back in the nineteen nineties.
It makes you wonder how a single wrong assumption can travel so much further than the truth that corrects it.
